body.p: Claims 1-12, 14 and 16 are now present in this application.
Claim 1 has been amended. Claims 13 and 15 have been cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer. Favorable consideration of the application, as amended, is respectfully requested.
Claim 1 has been amended, the support of which could be found at least in paragraph [0033] of the specification, as filed.
It is respectfully submitted that the foregoing amendments do not contain new matter. As such, the Examiner is respectfully requested to enter the same.

The drawings are objected to under 37 CFR 1.83(a). The drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims. Therefore, the tying place positioned on the supporting member (30) of claim 13 and the through hole arranged in the supporting member (30) of claim 15 must be shown or the feature(s) canceled from the claim(s).
Claims 13 and 15 have been cancelled.

In view of the foregoing amendments, it is respectfully submitted that these informalities have been addressed. Reconsideration and withdrawal of any objection to the drawings are respectfully requested.

Claim 15 is rejected under35 U.S.C.112(b) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention. This rejection is respectfully traversed.
Claim 15 has been cancelled. The rejection should be moot.
In view of the foregoing amendments, withdrawal of the 35 USC 112 rejection is respectfully requested.

Claims 1-3, 5-6, 8-12 and 14 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (a)(1) as being anticipated by Carpenter (US 4,354,647). Claims 1, 3-4, 7, 13 and 15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (a)(1) as being anticipated by Carlson et al. (US 2007/0084970 Al), hereinafter Carlson, as is evidenced by the "Pulixin Packaging Materials" Website. These rejections are respectfully traversed.

Applicant respectfully traverses the above objections. Furthermore, in view of the reasoning presented herein below, Applicant respectfully submits that Carpenter and Carlson, either alone or in combination, fails to teach or suggest all the claimed features as recited in Applicant's independent claim 1.
In particular, Carpenter and Carlson fail to teach or suggest the following feature of the amended independent claim 1 which recites,
"wherein the body of the kite includes a supporting member formed
directly from the wing, and
wherein the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing ".

The key feature of the present invention is that the supporting member is integrally formed directly from the wing, whereas in Carpenter, the supporting member (rib 17) is separate from the wing and is formed as a result of folding the body section 24, as described in column 4, lines 12- 19 and lines 41-53, and shown in Figure 7 and Figure 13. Carpenter's Figure 7 depicts a method in which the wing section 23 is attached to the now folded body section 24, which is distinct from the present invention where the supporting member is integrally formed directly from the wing itself. Carpenter's method of assembly inherently involves a separate formation and attachment process, making it distinct from the claimed invention that simplifies the structure by forming the supporting member directly from the wing. Therefore, Applicant submits that Carpenter does not disclose or anticipate "the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing" feature of the claimed invention.

Further, Applicant submits that Carpenter is directed towards kites of extremely small dimensions, as described in column 1, lines 31-35. The motivation in Carpenter is to provide a kite that can be folded and carried in a very small, compact form, which is a different motivation from the present invention. The present invention solves the problem of providing a kite that is simple in structure, easy to produce, low in production cost, and convenient to carry. These technical advantages are not addressed or solved by Carpenter, which is primarily focused on compactness and folding mechanisms. Therefore, since Carpenter does not disclose or suggest a supporting member formed directly from the wing as claimed, nor does it address the same problem solved by the present invention, amended independent claim 1 is not anticipated by Carpenter. Based on the above distinctions, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of amended independent

claim 1 over Carpenter be withdrawn. Claims 2, 3, 5-6, 8-12, and 14 depend on amended independent claim 1. Since amended independent claim 1 is not anticipated by Carpenter, the dependent claims are also not anticipated by the virtue of their dependency on amended independent claim 1. Accordingly, Applicant also requests withdrawal of the rejections of claims 2, 3, 5-6, 8-12, and 14.

Claim 1 has also been rejected as being anticipated by Carlson. However, Applicant respectfully submits that Carlson does not anticipate amended independent claim 1 for the reasons discussed below. In particular, Carpenter and Carlson fail to teach or suggest the following feature of the independent amended independent claim 1 which recites,
"wherein the body of the kite includes a supporting member formed
directly from the wing, and
wherein the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing."

Applicant submits that the present invention claims a supporting member formed directly from the wing. In contrast, Carlson discloses a kite where the supporting member (frame 2b) is bonded to the wing using adhesives, as described in paragraph [0021]. This bonding process inherently involves a separate supporting member that is affixed to the wing, rather than being an integral part of the wing itself. This is fundamentally different from the claimed invention, where the supporting member is integrally formed directly from the wing, simplifying the structure and enhancing the ease of production. Carlson's discussion of the supporting frame does not suggest or imply that the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing. Instead, the supporting member is a separate component that is attached to the wing using adhesives. Therefore, Applicant submits that Carlson does not disclose or anticipate "the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing" feature of the claimed invention.

Further, Applicant submits that Carlson is directed to solving the problem of high labour content in traditional kite designs, where each spar must be attached by hand to the sail. Carlson's focus on reducing labour in kite production is distinct from the technical problem addressed by the present invention, which is to provide a kite with a simple structure, low production cost, and convenient portability. The claimed invention simplifies the kite's structure by forming the supporting member directly from the wing, which is not addressed by Carlson's design involving separate components like multiple spars. Therefore, Carlson does not anticipate claim 1, as it does

not disclose the feature of a supporting member integrally formed directly from the wing, nor does it address the same technical problem solved by the present invention. In light of the above distinctions, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of amended independent claim 1 over Carlson be withdrawn. Claims 3, 4, 7, 13, and 15 depend on amended independent claim 1. Since amended independent claim 1 is not anticipated by Carlson, the dependent claims are also not anticipated by the virtue of their dependency on amended independent claim 1.

In view of the above arguments and distinctions between the cited prior art and the claimed invention, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) and allowance of claims 1-3, 5-6, 8-12, and 14 over Carpenter, and claims 1, 3-4, 7, 13, and 15 over Carlson. Reconsideration and withdrawal of the 35 USC 102 rejection(s) are respectfully requested.

The Examiner indicated that this application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U .S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.

Claim 16 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Carpenter. Additionally, claim 16 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Carlson. This rejection is respectfully traversed.
In response to the examiner's comment regarding the presumption of common ownership, Applicant confirms that:
1. This instant application (18/426,298) names a single inventor (Chi Kong PANG), who is
the same inventor as the parent application (17/295,056).
2. The subject matter of all claims in this continuation application was commonly owned by
the inventor as of the effective filing date of this application and the parent application.
3. There are no claims in this instant application that were not commonly owned as of the
effective filing date.
Accordingly, Applicant submits that the 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(2)(C) applies, and no prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(2) should be applied against the claims based on a lack of common ownership.

Further, Applicant has looked in the parent US application and see that the certified copy of the priority document HK18114984.9 is readily available. The Examiner should therefore be able to retrieve the priority document from the parent application.

Further, Applicant respectfully submits that independent claim 1 is non-obvious in view of Carpenter (US 4,354,647) and Carlson et al. (US 2007/0084970 Al). Specifically, Carpenter and Carlson fail to disclose the differentiating feature of amended independent claim 1 which recites:
"the body of the kite includes a supporting member formed directly
from the wing, and
the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing."
Applicant submits that neither Carpenter nor Carlson discloses or suggests this feature, and both references offer teachings that are fundamentally different from the claimed invention.

Applicant submits that Carpenter discloses a kite where the supporting member (rib 17) is formed through the process of folding a portion of the kite's body (col. 3, lines 34-39). However, Carpenter does not teach or suggest that the supporting member is formed directly from the wing itself or that it is integrally formed with the wing. Instead, the supporting member in Carpenter is a separate structural element that is created during the assembly process by folding and reinforcing the body section (24) of the kite, which then becomes a distinct rib (17) that helps maintain the kite's shape.

Further, Applicant submits that Carpenter's supporting member is not integrally formed with the wing but is instead created separately by folding a portion of the kite's body. This folding process results in a discrete rib that is added to the kite's structure, which is not structurally or functionally integrated with the wing in the manner claimed. The supporting member in claim 1 is formed directly from the wing, meaning it is an inseparable part of the wing itself, which is a key distinction from Carpenter.

Furthermore, Applicant submits that Carpenter's method of assembling the kite does not suggest that the supporting member is formed directly from the wing. The wing section (23) and the body section (24) are assembled as separate parts (column 4, lines 12-19 and lines 41-53, and

shown in Figure 7 and Figure 13), and there is no teaching that the supporting member is an integral part of the wing. In contrast, amended independent claim 1 specifies that the supporting member is directly formed from the wing itself, resulting in a structurally integrated component that is central to the kite's design.

Moreover, Applicant submits that Carpenter's objective is to create a small-sized kite with a reinforced rib to prevent collapse of the wing under certain flying conditions (col. 3, lines 36- 40). This objective is distinct from the claimed invention, which focuses on a simplified structure where the supporting member is integrally formed with the wing to improve mass production, reduce cost, and enhance portability. Carpenter's approach does not contemplate this type of structural integration between the wing and the supporting member.

Similarly, Applicant submits that Carlson discloses a kite where the supporting member (frame 2b) is a separate component that is attached to the body (sail lb) using adhesives (paragraph [0021]). Carlson's design relies on a multi-component frame that is bonded to the sail to provide rigidity. This is fundamentally different from the claimed differentiating feature where the supporting member is formed directly from the wing and is integrally formed with it.

Applicant submits that in Carlson, the supporting member is a distinct frame (2b) that is attached to the sail using adhesives or other assembly processes. There is no teaching or suggestion that the supporting member is formed directly from the wing or that it is integrally formed with the wing. Carlson's design involves multiple separate components that are assembled together, which contrasts with the claimed invention where the supporting member is an inseparable part of the wing.

Further, Applicant submits that Carlson's design focuses on reducing labour costs and simplifying production by using adhesive bonding to attach the frame to the sail (paragraph [0021]). This approach is fundamentally different from the claimed invention, which achieves structural simplicity by forming the supporting member directly from the wing. In contrast to Carlson's multi-component assembly, the claimed invention provides a single-piece wing and supporting member, which is easier to manufacture and more cost-effective.

Moreover, Applicant submits that Carlson is motivated by the need to simplify the assembly process and reduce the labour required to produce complex kites. The use of adhesives to bond the frame to the sail is consistent with this goal, but it does not suggest or teach the concept of forming the supporting member directly from the wing. Carlson's reliance on separate
components and adhesive bonding would not lead a person of ordinary skill in the art to integrally form the supporting member with the wing as claimed.

Applicant submits that neither reference suggests or teaches the structural simplicity achieved by forming the supporting member directly from the wing and integrally forming the two components. The claimed invention's combination of these features provides unexpected advantages in terms of ease of production, cost reduction, and flight stability, which are not disclosed or suggested by either Carpenter or Carlson.

Given the above distinctions, Applicant respectfully submits that amended independent claim 1 is non-obvious over the prior art of Carpenter and Carlson. Neither reference teaches or suggests the feature of a supporting member formed directly from the wing and integrally formed with the wing, and both references focus on different technical objectives that do not lead to the claimed invention. Therefore, in view of the above, Applicant respectfully submits that the amended independent claim 1 is inventive and non-obvious over Carpenter and Carlson or the combination thereof. Applicant submits that since Carpenter and Carlson fail to disclose or suggest said feature, thus the amended independent claim 1 and its dependent claims are patentable under 35 U.S.C. §103 in view of the combination of Carpenter, Carlson and the obvious general knowledge. Further, Applicant submits that dependent claims 2-12, 14 and 16 are also patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 by the virtue of their dependency on amended independent claim 1.

In addition, regarding the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner asserts that positioning the tying place closer to the outer edge of the wing than the supporting member, as claimed, would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art because rearranging parts of an invention involves only routine skill.

However, Applicant respectfully submits that this modification is not obvious in light of Carpenter. Applicant submits that Carpenter's Figure 10 shows the tying place (14c) located centrally on the body, attached to the yoke (13), which is placed away from the outer edge of the wing. Carpenter does not provide any suggestion or motivation to move the tying place closer to the outer edge of the wing as claimed in claim 16. The positioning of the tying place in Carpenter is optimized for the specific structure and aerodynamic properties of Carpenter's kite, particularly for its small-sized kite design. Relocating the tying place to the outer edge of the wing would fundamentally alter the function and balance of Carpenter's kite, which aims to prevent collapse of the wing under certain flying conditions (col. 3, lines 36-40).

Further, Claim 16 specifies that positioning the tying place closer to the outer edge of the wing improves windward effect and stability. This feature is not a trivial rearrangement of parts but is based on the discovery that moving the tying place affects the kite's aerodynamic performance in a way that enhances stability. Carpenter does not teach or suggest such a modification, and there is no indication that a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that moving the tying place would result in improved stability. In fact, Carpenter's design, with the tying place centrally located, is integral to the kite's ability to maintain flight, and there is no motivation or expectation of success in moving it to the outer edge.

Moreover, Carpenter teaches a kite of extremely small dimensions (col. 1, lines 5-8), where precise balancing and structural integrity are critical. The central location of the tying place in Carpenter's kite is designed to work in conjunction with the supporting member (rib 17) to prevent collapse and maintain the kite's shape. Moving the tying place to the outer edge would destabilize the kite's structure and potentially compromise its ability to fly, thereby teaching away from the claimed invention's focus on improved windward effect and stability.

Furthermore, the examiner has also rejected claim 16 as being unpatentable over Carlson under 35 U.S.C. § 103. The examiner asserts that positioning the tying place closer to the outer edge of the wing than the supporting member would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art and that rearranging parts of the kite involves only routine skill.

Applicant submits that Carlson is primarily concerned with reducing labor costs and simplifying production by using adhesives to bond components together (§[0018]). Carlson's kite design involves a multi-component frame (2b) that is adhered to the sail (lb) to provide structural support. The tying place (3) in Carlson is positioned centrally, where it connects the kite to the flying line (Fig. 6). There is no teaching or suggestion in Carlson that moving the tying place closer to the outer edge of the wing would provide any aerodynamic advantage or improved stability. Carlson's focus is on assembly efficiency, not on fine-tuning the kite's aerodynamic properties.

Further, Carlson does not provide any motivation or suggestion to modify the location of the tying place for the purpose of improving windward effect and stability. The claimed invention's discovery that positioning the tying place closer to the outer edge improves stability is not an obvious design choice based on Carlson. In fact, Carlson's centrally located tying place is a logical choice for its specific kite structure, which relies on the frame to maintain the kite's shape, and there is no suggestion in Carlson that such a modification would result in improved performance.

It is also worth noting that the relationship between the tying place and other structural elements of the kite, such as the supporting member, contribute to the kite's overall aerodynamic stability in a synergistic way. The position of the tying place near the outer edge of the wing allows it to work in concert with the supporting member to optimize the kite's performance. This subtle interaction results in a kite that not only maintains its shape under varying wind conditions but also exhibits enhanced maneuverability and efficiency in flight. The configuration claimed in claim 16 results in an unexpected improvement in the kite's performance under various wind conditions. The improved windward effect and stability are not merely the result of routine design changes but arise from a deeper understanding of how the forces of lift and drag interact with the kite's structure when the tying place is positioned in the aforementioned way. The positioning of the tying place as claimed provides a technical advantage that would not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art based on Carpenter's and Carlson's teachings.

Furthermore, even though the examiner cites In re Japikse to argue that rearranging parts is routine, Applicant emphasizes that in this case, a person skilled in the art would not be motivated to rearrange the tying place tying place closer to the outer edge of the wing as none of the prior arts teach, suggest or motivate towards such a placement of the tying place. Moreover, the specific rearrangement of the tying place provides unexpected advantages in terms of aerodynamic performance and stability, which go beyond mere routine skill as held by the examiner.

Applicant submits that since Carpenter and Carlson fail to disclose or suggest said feature, thus claim 16 is patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 in view of the alleged combination of Carpenter, Carlson and the obvious general knowledge.

Further, claim 16 is patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 based on its dependency on amended independent claim 1 which is inventive and non-obvious in view of the combination of Carpenter, Carlson and the obvious general knowledge.

In view of the foregoing remarks, it is respectfully submitted that the prior arts utilized by the Examiner fails to teach or suggest the features of claim 16. Reconsideration and withdrawal of the 35 USC 103 rejections are respectfully requested.
Claims 1, 2, and 8-9 are rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over of U.S. Patent No. 11,189,605 (reproduced below). This rejection is respectfully traversed.

While Applicant does not concede the appropriateness of the double patenting rejection, attached herewith is a Terminal Disclaimer. As such, reconsideration and withdrawal of the double patenting rejection are respectfully requested.
Favorable reconsideration and an early Notice of Allowance are earnestly solicited.

Because the additional prior art cited by the Examiner has been included merely to show the state of the prior art and has not been utilized to reject the claims, no further comments concerning these documents are considered necessary at this time.

Applicants have made a diligent effort to place the claims in condition for allowance.
